output.methodChoice: D (competing hypotheses) – the case turns on which rival explanation survives discriminating evidence (round split, tier split).
output.brief: The enrolment drop is mainly a yield problem, not an applicant-pool problem. Applications, admits and admit quality all rose. Yield fell about 7.5 points in both early action (processed on the old system, on time) and regular decision (the slow, new-portal round). That makes the portal delay an unlikely main cause. The drop is concentrated in the tiers where the merit awards were cut. Dean's awards fell from $14k to $9k and yield fell from 45% to 32%. Merit awards fell from $9k to $5k and yield fell from 45% to 32%. Presidential awards (unchanged) and no-award admits barely moved. So the scholarship schedule the Board approved is the most likely cause. The finance committee relied on a 2021 elasticity estimate that was wrong. I'm fairly confident, but this is not an experiment, and I haven't split the tiers by round. The portal and reader-shortage problems were real and hurt individual students, and the missing-transcript claim is unresolved. Replacing the director would punish the wrong party and rest on a wrong diagnosis. Next steps: take a modelled proposal to restore awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers to the finance committee before award letters go out. Separately, set a regular-decision turnaround target and check the transcript problem.
